{{神社| 名称=総社| 所在地=岡山県津山市総社427| 位置={{ウィキ座標2段度分秒|35|4|26.71|N|133|59|39.60|E|}}| 祭神=大己貴命| 創建=伝・欽明天皇25年（564年）| 社格=県社| 例祭=春季例祭：4月10日
秋季例祭：10月第2日曜日
新嘗祭（湯立神事）：12月10日| 本殿=中山造| 別名=美作総社宮、惣社大明神| 画像=[[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 06.jpg|260px]]
社殿}} {{Commonscat|Mimasaka-sojagu}} '''美作総社宮'''（みまさかそうじゃぐう）は、[[岡山県]][[津山市]]にある[[神社]]。正式名称は'''総社'''。祭神は[[大国主|大己貴命]]。[[近代社格制度|旧社格]]は県社。 == 概要 == 社伝によれば、[[欽明天皇]]25年（[[564年]]）に現在地より約1km西にある本館（ほんだて）に大己貴命を祀ったのが始まりとされる。 [[奈良時代]]初期の[[和銅]]6年（[[713年]]）に[[備前国]]北部6郡を分割し[[美作国]]が出来、和銅7年（[[714年]]）にはここに国府が置かれた。その後、美作国司により現在の亀甲山に遷座した。[[中山神社]]・[[高野神社]]など美作65郷全てを合祀し美作国総社と定めた。 現在の本殿は[[戦国時代 (日本)|戦国時代]]に造営され、国の[[重要文化財]]に指定されている。 ==文化財== ;重要文化財（国指定） *総社本殿 :戦国時代の[[永禄]]5年（[[1562年]]）[[毛利元就]]が戦勝の記念として再建した。[[江戸時代]]前期の[[明暦]]3年（[[1657年]]）に[[津山藩]]主[[森長継]]により大改修が行われた。この地方独自の[[中山造]]で、桁行三[[間]]・梁間三間・一重[[入母屋]]造・妻入、向拝一間・向唐破風造、[[こけら葺]]である。[[大正]]3年（[[1914年]]）4月17日（旧国宝）指定。 == 画像 == File:Mimasaka Sojagu 02.jpg|鳥居と参道 File:Mimasaka Sojagu 07.jpg|中山造の本殿（国の重要文化財） ==参考文献== *岡山県高等学校教育研究会社会科部会歴史分科会/編 『新版 岡山県の歴史散歩』 山川出版社 1991年 196ページ *現地説明板 ==外部リンク== *[http://www.okayama-jinjacho.or.jp/cgi-bin/jsearch.cgi?mode=detail&jcode=03018 総社]岡山県神社庁 {{DEFAULTSORT:みまさかそうしやくう}} [[Category:岡山県の神社]] [[Category:津山市]] [[Category:岡山県の重要文化財]] [[Category:岡山県の旧県社]] [[Category:総社]]

{{神社 |名称 = 総社 |画像 = [[ファイル:Mimasaka-soujagu shaden.JPG|280px]]
社殿（本殿は重要文化財） |所在地 = [[岡山県]][[津山市]]総社427 |位置 = {{ウィキ座標2段度分秒|35|04|26.70|N|133|59|39.47|E|region:JP-33_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=美作総社宮}} |祭神 = [[大国主|大己貴命]] |神体 = |社格 = [[美作国]][[総社]]
旧[[県社]] |創建 = （伝）[[欽明天皇]]25年（[[564年]]?） |本殿 = [[中山造]] |別名 = 美作総社宮、惣社大明神 |札所等 = 美作三大社 |例祭 = |神事 = 湯立神事（12月10日） }} [[ファイル:Mimasaka-soujagu torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|鳥居]] '''美作総社宮'''（みまさかそうじゃぐう）は、[[岡山県]][[津山市]]にある[[神社]]。正式名称は'''総社'''。[[美作国]][[総社]]で、[[近代社格制度|旧社格]]は[[県社]]。 == 祭神 == ; 主祭神 * '''[[大国主|大己貴命]]''' （おおなむちのみこと） ; 相殿神 * 鏡作命 （かがみつくりのみこと） - [[中山神社]]（美作国[[一宮]]）祭神 * [[ウガヤフキアエズ|鵜茅葺不合命]] （うがやふきあえずのみこと） - [[高野神社 (津山市二宮)|高野神社]]（美作国二宮）祭神 * 美作国内の神 == 歴史 == [[古代]]、[[国司]]は各国内の全ての神社を一宮から順に巡拝していた。これを効率化するため、各国の[[国府]]近くに国内の神を合祀した[[総社]]を設け、まとめて祭祀を行うようになった。当社はそのうちの[[美作国]]の総社にあたる。 社伝によれば、[[欽明天皇]]25年（[[564年]]?）に現在地より約1[[キロメートル|km]]西にある本館（ほんだて）に大己貴命を祀ったのが始まりという境内説明板。。ただしその根拠は不明で、室町時代末期までの当社の沿革は明らかでない。 [[奈良時代]]初期の[[和銅]]6年（[[713年]]）に[[備前国]]北部6郡を分割し[[美作国]]が設けられ、和銅7年（[[714年]]）には国府が置かれたと伝える。その後、美作[[国司]]により現在の亀甲山に遷座するとともに、[[中山神社]]・[[高野神社]]など美作国65郷全てを合祀し美作国総社と定められたという。[[鎌倉時代]]に入り国府は廃れたが、当社は美作三大社の一社として崇敬されたと伝える。 確かな文献により当社の沿革が明らかとなるのは、[[永禄]]12年（[[1569年]]）、当地に進出してきた[[毛利元就]]により所領が安堵されて以降である。その後は領主からの崇敬は篤く、[[江戸時代]]には[[津山藩|津山藩主]]の[[森氏]]・[[越前松平家|松平氏]]から社領の寄進も受けた。 [[明治維新]]後、[[近代社格制度]]において[[県社]]に列したほか、神饌幣帛料共進神社に指定された『岡山県の地名』総社項。。 == 境内 == [[ファイル:Mimasaka-soujagu honden.JPG|thumb|200px|left|本殿（国の重要文化財）]] * 本殿（重要文化財） : [[戦国時代 (日本)|戦国時代]]の[[永禄]]5年（[[1562年]]）[[毛利元就]]が戦勝の記念として再建した。[[江戸時代]]前期の[[明暦]]3年（[[1657年]]）に[[津山藩]]主[[森長継]]により大改修が行われた。 : この地方独自の[[中山造]]で、桁行三[[間]]・梁間三間・一重[[入母屋]]造・妻入、向拝一間・向唐破風造、[[こけら葺]]である。 {{-}} ファイル:Mimasaka-soujagu haiden.JPG|拝殿 == 摂末社 == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|摂末社]] * 天満神社 * 稲荷神社 * 南神社 * 御崎神社 == 祭事 == * 春季例祭 （[[4月10日]]） * 秋季例祭 （10月第2日曜日） * 新嘗祭 （[[12月10日]]） - 特殊神事の湯立神事が行われる == 文化財 == === 重要文化財（国指定） === * 本殿 - [[大正]]3年（[[1914年]]）4月17日、当時の[[古社寺保存法]]に基づき特別保護建造物（現行法の[[重要文化財]]に相当）に指定 == 現地情報 == ; 所在地 * [[岡山県]][[津山市]]総社427 ; 周辺 * 国府台寺 - 美作国府跡の位置にあたる == 脚注 == {{reflist}} == 参考文献 == * 現地説明板 * 『日本歴史地名体系 岡山県の地名』（[[平凡社]]）津山市 総社項 * 岡山県高等学校教育研究会社会科部会歴史分科会 編『新版 岡山県の歴史散歩』（山川出版社、1991年）196ページ == 外部リンク == {{Commonscat|Mimasaka-sojagu}} * [http://www.city.tsuyama.lg.jp/index.cfm/22,5208,116,371,html#ｿｳｼﾞｬﾎﾝﾃﾞﾝ 総社本殿]（津山市ホームページ） * [http://www.okayama-jinjacho.or.jp/cgi-bin/jsearch.cgi?mode=detail&jcode=03018 総社]（岡山県神社庁） {{神道 横}} {{DEFAULTSORT:みまさかそうしやくう}} [[Category:岡山県の神社]] [[Category:津山市]] [[Category:総社]] [[Category:岡山県の旧県社]] [[Category:岡山県の重要文化財]] [[Category:室町時代の建築]] [[Category:美作国|社みまさかそうしやくう]]

主祭神 * '''[[大国主|大己貴命]]''' （おおなむちのみこと） ; 相殿神 * 鏡作命 （かがみつくりのみこと） - [[中山神社]]（美作国[[一宮]]）祭神 * [[ウガヤフキアエズ|鵜茅葺不合命]] （うがやふきあえずのみこと） - [[高野神社 (津山市二宮)|高野神社]]（美作国二宮）祭神 * 美作国内の神 == 歴史 == [[古代]]、[[国司]]は各国内の全ての神社を一宮から順に巡拝していた。これを効率化するため、各国の[[国府]]近くに国内の神を合祀した[[総社]]を設け、まとめて祭祀を行うようになった。当社はそのうちの[[美作国]]の総社にあたる。 社伝によれば、[[欽明天皇]]25年（[[564年]]?）に現在地より約1[[キロメートル|km]]西にある本館（ほんだて）に大己貴命を祀ったのが始まりという境内説明板。。ただしその根拠は不明で、室町時代末期までの当社の沿革は明らかでない。 [[奈良時代]]初期の[[和銅]]6年（[[713年]]）に[[備前国]]北部6郡を分割し[[美作国]]が設けられ、和銅7年（[[714年]]）には国府が置かれたと伝える。その後、美作[[国司]]により現在の亀甲山に遷座するとともに、[[中山神社]]・[[高野神社]]など美作国65郷全てを合祀し美作国総社と定められたという。[[鎌倉時代]]に入り国府は廃れたが、当社は美作三大社の一社として崇敬されたと伝える。 確かな文献により当社の沿革が明らかとなるのは、[[永禄]]12年（[[1569年]]）、当地に進出してきた[[毛利元就]]により所領が安堵されて以降である。その後は領主からの崇敬は篤く、[[江戸時代]]には[[津山藩|津山藩主]]の[[森氏]]・[[越前松平家|松平氏]]から社領の寄進も受けた。 [[明治維新]]後、[[近代社格制度]]において[[県社]]に列したほか、神饌幣帛料共進神社に指定された『岡山県の地名』総社項。。 == 境内 == * 本殿（重要文化財） : [[戦国時代 (日本)|戦国時代]]の[[永禄]]5年（[[1562年]]）[[毛利元就]]が戦勝の記念として再建した。[[江戸時代]]前期の[[明暦]]3年（[[1657年]]）に[[津山藩]]主[[森長継]]により大改修が行われた。 : この地方独自の[[中山造]]で、桁行三[[間]]・梁間三間・一重[[入母屋]]造・妻入、向拝一間・向唐破風造、[[こけら葺]]である。 {{-}} File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|本殿（国の重要文化財） File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|拝殿 == 摂末社 == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|摂末社]] * 天満神社 * 稲荷神社 * 南神社 * 御崎神社 == 祭事 == * 春季例祭 （[[4月10日]]） * 秋季例祭 （10月第2日曜日） * 新嘗祭 （[[12月10日]]） - 特殊神事の湯立神事が行われる == 文化財 == === 重要文化財（国指定） === * 本殿 - [[大正]]3年（[[1914年]]）4月17日、当時の[[古社寺保存法]]に基づき特別保護建造物（現行法の[[重要文化財]]に相当）に指定 == 現地情報 == ; 所在地 * [[岡山県]][[津山市]]総社427 ; 周辺 * 国府台寺 - 美作国府跡の位置にあたる == 脚注 == {{reflist}} == 参考文献 == * 現地説明板 * 『日本歴史地名体系 岡山県の地名』（[[平凡社]]）津山市 総社項 * 岡山県高等学校教育研究会社会科部会歴史分科会 編『新版 岡山県の歴史散歩』（山川出版社、1991年）196ページ == 外部リンク == {{Commonscat|Mimasaka-sojagu}} * [http://www.city.tsuyama.lg.jp/index.cfm/22,5208,116,371,html#ｿｳｼﾞｬﾎﾝﾃﾞﾝ 総社本殿]（津山市ホームページ） * [http://www.okayama-jinjacho.or.jp/cgi-bin/jsearch.cgi?mode=detail&jcode=03018 総社]（岡山県神社庁） {{神道 横}} {{DEFAULTSORT:みまさかそうしやくう}} [[Category:岡山県の神社]] [[Category:津山市]] [[Category:総社]] [[Category:岡山県の旧県社]] [[Category:岡山県の重要文化財]] [[Category:室町時代の建築]] [[Category:美作国|社みまさかそうしやくう]]

主祭神 * '''[[大国主|大己貴命]]''' （おおなむちのみこと） ; 相殿神 * 鏡作命 （かがみつくりのみこと） - [[中山神社]]（美作国[[一宮]]）祭神 * [[ウガヤフキアエズ|鵜茅葺不合命]] （うがやふきあえずのみこと） - [[高野神社 (津山市二宮)|高野神社]]（美作国二宮）祭神 * 美作国内の神 == 歴史 == [[古代]]、[[国司]]は各国内の全ての神社を一宮から順に巡拝していた。これを効率化するため、各国の[[国府]]近くに国内の神を合祀した[[総社]]を設け、まとめて祭祀を行うようになった。当社はそのうちの[[美作国]]の総社にあたる。 社伝によれば、[[欽明天皇]]25年（[[564年]]?）に現在地より約1[[キロメートル|km]]西にある本館（ほんだて）に大己貴命を祀ったのが始まりという境内説明板。。ただしその根拠は不明で、室町時代末期までの当社の沿革は明らかでない。 [[奈良時代]]初期の[[和銅]]6年（[[713年]]）に[[備前国]]北部6郡を分割し[[美作国]]が設けられ、和銅7年（[[714年]]）には国府が置かれたと伝える。その後、美作[[国司]]により現在の亀甲山に遷座するとともに、[[中山神社]]・[[高野神社]]など美作国65郷全てを合祀し美作国総社と定められたという。[[鎌倉時代]]に入り国府は廃れたが、当社は美作三大社の一社として崇敬されたと伝える。 確かな文献により当社の沿革が明らかとなるのは、[[永禄]]12年（[[1569年]]）、当地に進出してきた[[毛利元就]]により所領が安堵されて以降である。その後は領主からの崇敬は篤く、[[江戸時代]]には[[津山藩|津山藩主]]の[[森氏]]・[[越前松平家|松平氏]]から社領の寄進も受けた。 [[明治維新]]後、[[近代社格制度]]において[[県社]]に列したほか、神饌幣帛料供進神社に指定された『岡山県の地名』総社項。。 == 境内 == * 本殿（重要文化財） : [[戦国時代 (日本)|戦国時代]]の[[永禄]]5年（[[1562年]]）[[毛利元就]]が戦勝の記念として再建した。[[江戸時代]]前期の[[明暦]]3年（[[1657年]]）に[[津山藩]]主[[森長継]]により大改修が行われた。 : この地方独自の[[中山造]]で、桁行三[[間]]・梁間三間・一重[[入母屋]]造・妻入、向拝一間・向唐破風造、[[こけら葺]]である。 {{-}} File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|本殿（国の重要文化財） File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|拝殿 == 摂末社 == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|摂末社]] * 天満神社 * 稲荷神社 * 南神社 * 御崎神社 == 祭事 == * 春季例祭 （[[4月10日]]） * 秋季例祭 （10月第2日曜日） * 新嘗祭 （[[12月10日]]） - 特殊神事の湯立神事が行われる == 文化財 == === 重要文化財（国指定） === * 本殿 - [[大正]]3年（[[1914年]]）4月17日、当時の[[古社寺保存法]]に基づき特別保護建造物（現行法の[[重要文化財]]に相当）に指定 == 現地情報 == ; 所在地 * [[岡山県]][[津山市]]総社427 ; 周辺 * 国府台寺 - 美作国府跡の位置にあたる == 脚注 == {{reflist}} == 参考文献 == * 現地説明板 * 『日本歴史地名体系 岡山県の地名』（[[平凡社]]）津山市 総社項 * 岡山県高等学校教育研究会社会科部会歴史分科会 編『新版 岡山県の歴史散歩』（山川出版社、1991年）196ページ == 外部リンク == {{Commonscat|Mimasaka-sojagu}} * [http://www.city.tsuyama.lg.jp/index.cfm/22,5208,116,371,html#ｿｳｼﾞｬﾎﾝﾃﾞﾝ 総社本殿]（津山市ホームページ） * [http://www.okayama-jinjacho.or.jp/cgi-bin/jsearch.cgi?mode=detail&jcode=03018 総社]（岡山県神社庁） {{神道 横}} {{DEFAULTSORT:みまさかそうしやくう}} [[Category:岡山県の神社]] [[Category:津山市]] [[Category:津山市の歴史]] [[Category:総社]] [[Category:岡山県の旧県社]] [[Category:岡山県の重要文化財]] [[Category:室町時代の建築]] [[Category:美作国|社0]]

主祭神 * '''[[大国主|大己貴命]]''' （おおなむちのみこと） ; 相殿神 * 鏡作命 （かがみつくりのみこと） - [[中山神社]]（美作国[[一宮]]）祭神 * [[ウガヤフキアエズ|鵜茅葺不合命]] （うがやふきあえずのみこと） - [[高野神社 (津山市二宮)|高野神社]]（美作国二宮）祭神 * 美作国内の神 == 歴史 == [[古代]]、[[国司]]は各国内の全ての神社を一宮から順に巡拝していた。これを効率化するため、各国の[[国府]]近くに国内の神を合祀した[[総社]]を設け、まとめて祭祀を行うようになった。当社はそのうちの[[美作国]]の総社にあたる。 社伝によれば、[[欽明天皇]]25年（[[564年]]?）に現在地より約1[[キロメートル|km]]西にある本館（ほんだて）に大己貴命を祀ったのが始まりという境内説明板。。ただしその根拠は不明で、室町時代末期までの当社の沿革は明らかでない。 [[奈良時代]]初期の[[和銅]]6年（[[713年]]）に[[備前国]]北部6郡を分割し[[美作国]]が設けられ、和銅7年（[[714年]]）には国府が置かれたと伝える。その後、美作[[国司]]により現在の亀甲山に遷座するとともに、[[中山神社]]・[[高野神社]]など美作国65郷全てを合祀し美作国総社と定められたという。[[鎌倉時代]]に入り国府は廃れたが、当社は美作三大社の一社として崇敬されたと伝える。 確かな文献により当社の沿革が明らかとなるのは、[[永禄]]12年（[[1569年]]）、当地に進出してきた[[毛利元就]]により所領が安堵されて以降である。その後は領主からの崇敬は篤く、[[江戸時代]]には[[津山藩|津山藩主]]の[[森氏]]・[[越前松平家|松平氏]]から社領の寄進も受けた。 [[明治維新]]後、[[近代社格制度]]において[[県社]]に列したほか、神饌幣帛料供進神社に指定された『岡山県の地名』総社項。。 == 境内 == * 本殿（重要文化財） : [[戦国時代 (日本)|戦国時代]]の[[永禄]]5年（[[1562年]]）[[毛利元就]]が戦勝の記念として再建した。[[江戸時代]]前期の[[明暦]]3年（[[1657年]]）に[[津山藩]]主[[森長継]]により大改修が行われた。 : この地方独自の[[中山造]]で、桁行三[[間]]・梁間三間・一重[[入母屋]]造・妻入、向拝一間・向唐破風造、[[こけら葺]]である。 {{-}} File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|本殿（国の重要文化財） File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|拝殿 == 摂末社 == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|摂末社]] * 天満神社 * 稲荷神社 * 南神社 * 御崎神社 == 祭事 == * 春季例祭 （[[4月10日]]） * 秋季例祭 （10月第2日曜日） * 新嘗祭 （[[12月10日]]） - 特殊神事の湯立神事が行われる == 文化財 == === 重要文化財（国指定） === * 本殿 - [[大正]]3年（[[1914年]]）4月17日、当時の[[古社寺保存法]]に基づき特別保護建造物（現行法の[[重要文化財]]に相当）に指定 == 現地情報 == ; 所在地 * [[岡山県]][[津山市]]総社427 ; 周辺 * 国府台寺 - 美作国府跡の位置にあたる == 脚注 == {{脚注ヘルプ}} {{reflist}} == 参考文献 == * 現地説明板 * 『日本歴史地名体系 岡山県の地名』（[[平凡社]]）津山市 総社項 * 岡山県高等学校教育研究会社会科部会歴史分科会 編『新版 岡山県の歴史散歩』（山川出版社、1991年）196ページ == 外部リンク == {{Commonscat|Mimasaka-sojagu}} * [http://www.city.tsuyama.lg.jp/index.cfm/22,5208,116,371,html#ｿｳｼﾞｬﾎﾝﾃﾞﾝ 総社本殿]（津山市ホームページ） * [http://www.okayama-jinjacho.or.jp/cgi-bin/jsearch.cgi?mode=detail&jcode=03018 総社]（岡山県神社庁） {{神道 横}} {{DEFAULTSORT:みまさかそうしやくう}} [[Category:岡山県の神社]] [[Category:津山市の歴史]] [[Category:総社]] [[Category:岡山県の旧県社]] [[Category:岡山県の重要文化財]] [[Category:室町時代の建築]] [[Category:美作国|社0]] [[Category:津山市の建築物]]

{{Shrine | Name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | Address = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | Latitude = 35.074083 | Longitude = 133.994297 | Deities = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en|大国主}} | Map = Japan Okayama | Founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | Rank = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | Festivals = {{nihongo|Spring Festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn Festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest Festival)|December 10}} | Main Hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | Image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (Main Hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|en|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|en|近代社格制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * {{ill|Ugaya Fukiaezu|en|鵜茅葺不合命}} (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|en|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|en|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place Names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. Shrine Hall (Main Hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|en|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|en|近代社格制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * {{ill|Ugaya Fukiaezu|en|鵜茅葺不合命}} (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|en|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|en|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; **Main Hall (Honden)** * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. Shrine Hall (Main Hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|en|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|en|近代社格制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * {{ill|Ugaya Fukiaezu|en|鵜茅葺不合命}} (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|en|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|en|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; **Main Hall (Honden)** * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|Main Hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == Festivals == * **Spring Festival** (April 10) * **Autumn Festival** (Second Sunday in October) * **Niinamesai** (Harvest Festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * **Main Hall** – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == Location and Surroundings == ; **Address** * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; **Nearby landmarks** * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|en|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|en|近代社格制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * {{ill|Ugaya Fukiaezu|en|鵜茅葺不合命}} (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|en|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|en|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; **main hall (Honden)** * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|en|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|en|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * {{ill|Ugaya Fukiaezu|en|鵜茅葺不合命}} (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|en|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|en|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; **main hall (Honden)** * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|en|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|en|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * {{ill|Ugaya Fukiaezu|en|鵜茅葺不合命}} (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|en|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|en|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; **main hall (Honden)** * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|en|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|en|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * {{ill|Ugaya Fukiaezu|en|鵜茅葺不合命}} (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|en|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|en|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; **main hall (Honden)** * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|en|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|en|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * {{ill|Ugaya Fukiaezu|en|鵜茅葺不合命}} (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|en|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|en|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; **main hall (Honden)** * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * **Spring festival** (April 10) * **Autumn festival** (Second Sunday in October) * **Niinamesai** (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * **main hall** – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; **location** * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; **Nearby landmarks** * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|en|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|en|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * {{ill|Ugaya Fukiaezu|en|鵜茅葺不合命}} (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|en|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|en|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; **main hall (Honden)** * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * **Spring festival** (April 10) * **Autumn festival** (Second Sunday in October) * **Niinamesai** (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * **main hall** – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; **location** * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; **Nearby landmarks** * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). Heibonsha. * Okayama Prefectural High School Social Studies Department History Section, ''Revised Edition: History Walks in Okayama Prefecture,'' Yamakawa Publishing, 1991, p. 196. == External Links == * [http://www.city.tsuyama.lg.jp/index.cfm/22,5208,116,371,html#ｿｳｼﾞｬﾎﾝﾃﾞﾝ Sōja main hall] (Tsuyama City Website) * [http://www.okayama-jinjacho.or.jp/cgi-bin/jsearch.cgi?mode=detail&jcode=03018 {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|en|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|en|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|en|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|en|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; **main hall (Honden)** * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * **Spring festival** (April 10) * **Autumn festival** (Second Sunday in October) * **Niinamesai** (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * **main hall** – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; **location** * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; **Nearby landmarks** * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|en|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|en|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|en|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|en|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; **main hall (Honden)** * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * **Spring festival** (April 10) * **Autumn festival** (Second Sunday in October) * **Niinamesai** (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * **main hall** – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; **location** * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; **Nearby landmarks** * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). Heibonsha. * Okayama Prefectural High School Social Studies Department History Section, ''Revised Edition: History Walks in Okayama Prefecture,'' Yamakawa Publishing, 1991, p. 196. == External Links == * [http://www.city.tsuyama.lg.jp/index.cfm/22,5208,116,371,html#ｿｳｼﾞｬﾎﾝﾃﾞﾝ Sōja main hall] (Tsuyama City Website) * [http://www.okayama-jinjacho.or.jp/cgi-bin/jsearch.cgi?mode=detail&jcode=03018 {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; **main hall (Honden)** * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * **Spring festival** (April 10) * **Autumn festival** (Second Sunday in October) * **Niinamesai** (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * **main hall** – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; **location** * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; **Nearby landmarks** * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). Heibonsha. * Okayama Prefectural High School Social Studies Department History Section, ''Revised Edition: History Walks in Okayama Prefecture,'' Yamakawa Publishing, 1991, p. 196. == External Links == * [http://www.city.tsuyama.lg.jp/index.cfm/22,5208,116,371,html#ｿｳｼﾞｬﾎﾝﾃﾞﾝ Sōja main hall] (Tsuyama City Website) * [http://www.okayama-jinjacho.or.jp/cgi-bin/jsearch.cgi?mode=detail&jcode=03018 {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; **main hall (Honden)** * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * **Spring festival** (April 10) * **Autumn festival** (Second Sunday in October) * **Niinamesai** (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * **main hall** – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; **location** * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; **Nearby landmarks** * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; **main hall (Honden)** * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * **Spring festival** (April 10) * **Autumn festival** (Second Sunday in October) * **Niinamesai** (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * **main hall** – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; **location** * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; **Nearby landmarks** * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; '''main hall (Honden)''' * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * '''Spring festival''' (April 10) * '''Autumn festival''' (Second Sunday in October) * '''Niinamesai''' (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * '''main hall''' – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; '''location''' * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; '''Nearby landmarks''' * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; '''main hall (Honden)''' * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * '''Spring festival''' (April 10) * '''Autumn festival''' (Second Sunday in October) * '''Niinamesai''' (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * '''main hall''' – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; '''location''' * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; '''Nearby landmarks''' * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). Heibonsha. * Okayama Prefectural High School Social Studies Department History Section, ''Revised Edition: History Walks in Okayama Prefecture,'' Yamakawa Publishing, 1991, p. 196. == External Links
