{{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; '''main hall (Honden)''' * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * '''Spring festival''' (April 10) * '''Autumn festival''' (Second Sunday in October) * '''Niinamesai''' (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * '''main hall''' – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; '''location''' * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; '''Nearby landmarks''' * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; '''main hall (Honden)''' * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * '''Spring festival''' (April 10) * '''Autumn festival''' (Second Sunday in October) * '''Niinamesai''' (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * '''main hall''' – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; '''location''' * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; '''Nearby landmarks''' * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; '''main hall (Honden)''' * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * '''Spring festival''' (April 10) * '''Autumn festival''' (Second Sunday in October) * '''Niinamesai''' (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * '''main hall''' – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; '''location''' * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; '''Nearby landmarks''' * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; '''main hall (Honden)''' * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * '''Spring festival''' (April 10) * '''Autumn festival''' (Second Sunday in October) * '''Niinamesai''' (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * '''main hall''' – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; '''location''' * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; '''Nearby landmarks''' * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). Heibonsha. * Okayama Prefectural High School Social Studies Department History Section, ''Revised Edition: History Walks in Okayama Prefecture,'' Yamakawa Publishing, 1991, p. 196. == External Links == * [http://www.city.tsuyama.lg.jp/index.cfm/22,5208,116,371,html#ｿｳｼﾞｬﾎﾝﾃﾞﾝ Sōja main hall] (Tsuyama City Website) * [http://www.okayama-jinjacho.or.jp/cgi-bin/jsearch.cgi?mode=detail&jcode=03018 {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; '''main hall (Honden)''' * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * '''Spring festival''' (April 10) * '''Autumn festival''' (Second Sunday in October) * '''Niinamesai''' (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * '''main hall''' – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; '''location''' * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; '''Nearby landmarks''' * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; '''main hall (Honden)''' * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * '''Spring festival''' (April 10) * '''Autumn festival''' (Second Sunday in October) * '''Niinamesai''' (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * '''main hall''' – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; '''location''' * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; '''Nearby landmarks''' * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). Heibonsha. * Okayama Prefectural High School Social Studies Department History Section, ''Revised Edition: History Walks in Okayama Prefecture,'' Yamakawa Publishing, 1991, p. 196. == External Links == * [http://www.city.tsuyama.lg.jp/index.cfm/22,5208,116,371,html#ｿｳｼﾞｬﾎﾝﾃﾞﾝ Sōja main hall] (Tsuyama City Website) * [http://www.okayama-jinjacho.or.jp/cgi-bin/jsearch.cgi?mode=detail&jcode=03018 {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; '''main hall (Honden)''' * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * '''Spring festival''' (April 10) * '''Autumn festival''' (Second Sunday in October) * '''Niinamesai''' (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * '''main hall''' – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; '''location''' * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; '''Nearby landmarks''' * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). Heibonsha. * Okayama Prefectural High School Social Studies Department History Section, ''Revised Edition: History Walks in Okayama Prefecture,'' Yamakawa Publishing, 1991, p. 196. == External Links == * [http://www.city.tsuyama.lg.jp/index.cfm/22,5208,116,371,html#ｿｳｼﾞｬﾎﾝﾃﾞﾝ Sōja main hall] (Tsuyama City Website) * [http://www.okayama-jinjacho.or.jp/cgi-bin/jsearch.cgi?mode=detail&jcode=03018 {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; '''main hall (Honden)''' * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * '''Spring festival''' (April 10) * '''Autumn festival''' (Second Sunday in October) * '''Niinamesai''' (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * '''main hall''' – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; '''location''' * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; '''Nearby landmarks''' * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; '''main hall (Honden)''' * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * '''Spring festival''' (April 10) * '''Autumn festival''' (Second Sunday in October) * '''Niinamesai''' (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * '''main hall''' – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; '''location''' * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; '''Nearby landmarks''' * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). Heibonsha. * Okayama Prefectural High School Social Studies Department History Section, ''Revised Edition: History Walks in Okayama Prefecture,'' Yamakawa Publishing, 1991, p. 196. == External Links == * [http://www.city.tsuyama.lg.jp/index.cfm/22,5208,116,371,html#ｿｳｼﾞｬﾎﾝﾃﾞﾝ Sōja main hall] (Tsuyama City Website) * [http://www.okayama-jinjacho.or.jp/cgi-bin/jsearch.cgi?mode=detail&jcode=03018 {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}

Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; '''main hall (Honden)''' * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * '''Spring festival''' (April 10) * '''Autumn festival''' (Second Sunday in October) * '''Niinamesai''' (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * '''main hall''' – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; '''location''' * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; '''Nearby landmarks''' * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; '''main hall (Honden)''' * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * '''Spring festival''' (April 10) * '''Autumn festival''' (Second Sunday in October) * '''Niinamesai''' (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * '''main hall''' – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; '''location''' * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; '''Nearby landmarks''' * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; '''main hall (Honden)''' * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * '''Spring festival''' (April 10) * '''Autumn festival''' (Second Sunday in October) * '''Niinamesai''' (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * '''main hall''' – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; '''location''' * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; '''Nearby landmarks''' * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; '''main hall (Honden)''' * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * '''Spring festival''' (April 10) * '''Autumn festival''' (Second Sunday in October) * '''Niinamesai''' (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * '''main hall''' – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; '''location''' * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; '''Nearby landmarks''' * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; '''main hall (Honden)''' * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * '''Spring festival''' (April 10) * '''Autumn festival''' (Second Sunday in October) * '''Niinamesai''' (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * '''main hall''' – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; '''location''' * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; '''Nearby landmarks''' * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Mimasaka Sōjagū | location = 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, [[Okayama Prefecture]] | type = 35.074083 | longitude = 133.994297 | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主}} | map = Japan Okayama | founded = {{nihongo|25th year of Emperor Kinmei's reign|564 CE?}} | type = Former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]] | Structure = [[Nakayama-zukuri]] | festivals = {{nihongo|Spring festival|April 10}}
{{nihongo|Autumn festival|Second Sunday of October}}
{{nihongo|Niinamesai (Harvest festival)|December 10}} | main hall = Important Cultural Property of Japan | image = [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū shaden.JPG|280px]]
Shrine Hall (main hall is an Important Cultural Property) }} [[File:Mimasaka-soujagū torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii gate]] '''Mimasaka Sōjagū''' ({{lang|ja|美作総社宮}}) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en}} located in {{ill|Tsuyama|en}}, [[Okayama Prefecture]], Japan. It served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (regional shrine) of the former {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}, bringing together the deities of various local shrines. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代rank制度}}, it was designated as a former [[Prefectural Shrine|Prefectural Shrine]]. == Deities == ; Main deity * {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}} (Ōnamuchi no Mikoto) ; Enshrined deities * {{ill|Kagami-tsukuri no Mikoto|en}} (deity of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|ja|中山神社}}, the ichinomiya of Mimasaka Province) * [[Ugayafukiaezu]] (deity of {{ill|Takano Shrine|ja|高野神社}}, the ninomiya of Mimasaka Province) * Deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts == History == In ancient Japan, provincial governors ({{ill|Kokushi|ja|国司}}) were tasked with visiting all the shrines within their jurisdiction. To simplify this process, regional shrines (sōja) were established near provincial capitals (kokufu), consolidating the worship of local deities. Mimasaka Sōjagū served as the sōja for {{ill|Mimasaka Province|en}}. According to tradition, the shrine was established in 564 CE during the reign of {{nihongo|Emperor Kinmei|欽明天皇}}, with Ōkuninushi enshrined at a location approximately 1 km west of its current site, known as {{nihongo|Hondate|本館}}.Information board at the shrine. Later, during the early {{nihongo|Nara period|710–794}}, the provincial government relocated the shrine to its current location on {{nihongo|Kamegase Mountain|亀甲山}}, consolidating the deities from Mimasaka's 65 districts, including those of {{ill|Nakayama Shrine|en}} and {{ill|Takano Shrine|en}}. During the {{nihongo|Kamakura period|1185–1333}}, although the provincial government diminished in importance, the shrine remained a center of worship and became one of Mimasaka's "Three Great Shrines" ({{nihongo|Mimasaka Sandai-sha|美作三大社}}). Historical records confirm the shrine's continuity from 1569 when {{ill|Mōri Motonari|en}} granted land to the shrine.''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名), entry for Sōja. During the {{nihongo|Edo period|1603–1868}}, the shrine was supported by the {{ill|Mori clan|en}} and later the {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en}}, rulers of the {{ill|Tsuyama Domain|en}}, who made significant contributions to its upkeep. It was designated as a Prefectural Shrine in the {{nihongo|Meiji period|1868–1912}} and included in the list of government-supported shrines. == Shrine Buildings == ; '''main hall (Honden)''' * Built in 1562 by Mōri Motonari to commemorate a military victory and extensively renovated in 1657 by {{ill|Mori Nagatsugu|en}}, lord of the Tsuyama Domain. * Features the unique {{nihongo|Nakayama-zukuri|中山造}} architectural style: three-bay-wide and three-bay-deep, with a single-story gabled structure. It is designated as an {{ill|Important Cultural Property of Japan|en}}. File:Mimasaka-soujagū honden.JPG|main hall (Important Cultural Property) File:Mimasaka-soujagū haiden.JPG|Worship Hall (Haiden) == Auxiliary Shrines == [[File:Mimasaka Sojagu 08.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Auxiliary shrines]] * Tenman Shrine * Inari Shrine * Minami Shrine * Misaki Shrine == festivals == * '''Spring festival''' (April 10) * '''Autumn festival''' (Second Sunday in October) * '''Niinamesai''' (Harvest festival, December 10) – Includes the unique {{nihongo|Yutate Shinto Ritual|湯立神事}}, where water is boiled as an offering to the deities. == Cultural Properties == === Important Cultural Properties of Japan === * '''main hall''' – Designated in 1914 under the {{ill|Ancient Shrines and Temples Preservation Law|en}} (now {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|en}}). == location and Surroundings == ; '''location''' * 427 Sōja, Tsuyama City, Okayama Prefecture ; '''Nearby landmarks''' * Kokufudai Temple – Site of the former Mimasaka provincial capital (kokufu). == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Information board at the shrine. * ''Okayama Prefecture Place names'' (岡山県の地名). Heibonsha. * Okayama Prefectural High School Social Studies Department History Section, ''Revised Edition: History Walks in Okayama Prefecture,'' Yamakawa Publishing, 1991, p. 196. == External Links == * [http://www.city.tsuyama.lg.jp/index.cfm/22,5208,116,371,html#ｿｳｼﾞｬﾎﾝﾃﾞﾝ Sōja main hall] (Tsuyama City Website) * [http://www.okayama-jinjacho.or.jp/cgi-bin/jsearch.cgi?mode=detail&jcode=03018
